text: The Weesp train disaster occurred on 13 September 1918 near Weesp, Netherlands, and was the largest train disaster in Dutch railway history until the 1962 Harmelen train disaster. The 102 train, traveling from Amersfoort to Amsterdam, derailed near the railway bridge over the Merwedekanaal after the dike subsided over a length of 95 metres while ascending the slope of Weesp station. This subsidence, caused by extensive rainfall in the preceding period and the poor condition of the railway dike, happened at 10:25 when the locomotive was already on the bridge and became entangled in the ironworks of the bridge construction. The locomotive and tender flipped to the right, with the tender lying on the bridgehead and a luggage wagon coming to a standstill beside it. The following three carriages slid off the slope and collided, with their wooden upper sides largely splintered, resulting in many casualties. The third carriage was engulfed by the luggage and postal carriages, the latter partially ending up next to the forward carriages, while the carriage behind the postal carriage ended up skewed down from the slope but was barely damaged. The rear carriages derailed but remained on the tracks. Two minutes before the disaster, a train from Amsterdam to Hilversum passed through. The station chief sounded the alarm at 10:45. A surgeon on the train provided first aid, later assisted by two doctors from Weesp, and four nuns and soldiers from the neighborhood also helped. There were no fatalities among the train crew, who also assisted immediately after the accident. The first aid train arrived from Naarden-Bussum at 11:40, followed by accident carriages and transport carriages for injured passengers from Amsterdam. By 12:40, injured and non-injured passengers could leave for Amsterdam. About 2.5 hours after the disaster, the first injured arrived at Muiderpoort station in Amsterdam and were transferred to the Onze Lieve Vrouwe Gasthuis hospital. Two ships on the Merwedekanaal were stopped and transported injured to the Binnengasthuis. At 13:30, a tug departed with two ships and 36 injured for Amsterdam; half an hour later, a ship carrying 32 corpses arrived at the Wilhelmina Gasthuis at 16:00. One of the victims was Henri Gorter, a Dutch cyclist, speed skater, and ice skates manufacturer from Zwolle, who died that evening at the Binnengasthuis. Trains between Amsterdam and Amersfoort were rerouted through Breukelen and Utrecht, with commuter trains running from Naarden-Bussum via Hilversum and Utrecht to Amsterdam. Rail traffic resumed over one track six days after the disaster at a maximum speed of five km/h, and both tracks were fully restored on 2 December after the bridge and dike were repaired. A day after the disaster, an investigative commission chaired by minister Lely was formed, concluding that the embankment had been saturated by prolonged rainfall, worsened by impenetrable layers in the dike that prevented water from escaping, and by seepage from the Merwedekanaal through the loam dikes, raising the groundwater level above ground. The train's passage caused vibrations that led to the collapse of the liquefied dike. The disaster led to the founding of the Laboratorium voor Grondmechanica at the Technische Hogeschool in Delft and accelerated Albert Sybrandus Keverling Buisman’s soil mechanics research. On 19 June 1953, two passenger trains collided near Weesp, resulting in at least two deaths. The coordinates of the disaster site are 52°19′28″N 5°01′06″E / 52.32444°N 5.01833°E / 52.32444; 5.01833.
